description: Site-specific parameter knowledge. Keys use official FATES/ELM names. PFT specificity stored in parameter_pft and affects_pfts fields.

insights: Controls PFT fine root steady-state biomass
For PFT#10, low value (5e-06, locked) accidentally outperformed high value (0.001, responsive) due to PID responding to wrong stress signal when total productivity extremely low
PID controller only active when NPP is positive. Irrelevant during early spring carbon deficit period
Controls hierarchical feedback mechanism - monitors C:nutrient storage ratio and adjusts l2fr allocation, not directly controlled by vmax_p
Higher values trigger allocation paradox through PID feedback system - can decrease total P uptake despite higher per-root capacity
Maxed out at upper bound (5e-06) in best case, with uptake 100,000x too low for demand
10x increase causes only minor biomass decline (-12% fineroot) compared to vmax_p catastrophic effects
At maximum Morris value (5.0e-05) but maxed out - phosphatase production insufficient for organic P extraction
For PFT#10: fraction of phosphatase production going to plant (0.0170) too low. Need 10x increase but capped at <1.0 since it is a fraction
For PFT#7: counterintuitively NEGATIVE for leaf biomass despite increasing P availability, due to carbon costs
For PFT#10: setting to 3.0 works synergistically with phenology and PID modifications - storage alone insufficient but critical component
For PFT#10: Arctic graminoids need high C storage for 9-month winter survival
For PFT#9: increasing from 0.887 to 1.40 is the key driver for biomass improvement and MODIS LAI/GPP optimization, providing C stress buffering
Higher specific leaf area (thinner leaves) improves graminoid performance
At maximum Morris value - thin, high-area leaves typical of graminoids to maximize light capture per unit C
For PFT#10: higher photosynthetic capacity needed for graminoids in short Arctic growing season
For PFT#9: 40% higher Vcmax (81.8 vs 58.4 between cases) still underestimates PFT#9 biomass, indicating photosynthetic capacity is not the limiting factor
5 orders of magnitude range captures extreme niche differentiation in NH4 uptake strategies - bounds are adequate and should NOT be extended
PFT#9 and PFT#10 have opposite bounds for NH4 uptake, creating competitive niche differentiation
PFT#9 crown area parameter with strong cross-PFT competition effect on PFT#10 fineroot biomass through light competition
Works synergistically with chill temperature - both must be calibrated together from compatible parameter regimes
Shared phenology parameter across all PFTs, calibrated value -0.010246939908027598
Must be calibrated from representative cases in successful parameter space rather than using universal values
Shared phenology parameter across all PFTs, calibrated value 2.9964172939383626
Large coefficient (638) that amplifies exponential term changes - acts as multiplier making phen_c extremely sensitive
GDD threshold intercept (-68 C-days) - negative value allows exponential term to dominate threshold calculation
Shows opposite constraints between cases - Case #2675 at upper bound vs Case #3643 at lower bound, creating different spring carbon dynamics
Reducing by 90% causes ecosystem collapse - maintenance respiration is necessary for tissue maintenance
Minimal effect on leaf biomass - only +2% improvement for PFT#10 when increased by 40%
At lower bounds in best cases - graminoid growth form mismatches DBH-based allometry
No effect on annual mean biomass values - consistently tested across multiple series with identical results

Controls ecosystem growing season length and creates fundamental trade-off. -7.46 C gives good biomass but 2-3x LAI overestimate. +2.92 C matches MODIS but loses PFT#9. 10.4 C difference between cases.
Typically 2.0-2.4, provides 65-72% MR reduction at 5 C vs 20 C reference, but reduction insufficient for Arctic spring conditions
Controls mineralization rates and microbial competition
For PFT#7: Case #845 uses 380.0 vs Case #2675 uses 240.0 - higher values increase microbial competition and suppress PFT performance
For PFT#10: creates opposite competition effects between cases. High value (340) suppresses PFT#10 despite good P uptake. Low value (180) allows PFT#10 to dominate despite lower P uptake.
For PFT#9: at upper bound (420) in Case #845, shows extreme microbial competition strategies between best cases
Background mortality inversely related to competitive ability - higher mortality for dominant PFT enables coexistence
Lower bounds expanded for all PFTs to allow broader exploration of seed decay rates
For PFT#9: reducing from 0.731 to 0.32 enables recruitment to replenish mortality losses
For PFT#10: lower decay rate compensates for missing vegetative reproduction in FATES - seeds are only reproduction pathway
2D parameter with organ x PFT dimensions, requires organ index (1=leaf) for modification
For PFT#10 leaf: at maximum Morris value (0.0407) - maximizing N in leaves for photosynthetic capacity under P limitation
For PFT#9 fineroot: measurement-constrained at lower bound - DO NOT extend without additional field data from Salmon et al studies
2D parameter with organ x PFT dimensions, requires organ index (1=leaf) for modification
For PFT#10 leaf: at minimum Morris value (0.000921) - minimizing P in leaves to conserve scarce P for root P acquisition
For PFT#10 fineroot: measurement-constrained at upper bound indicates P specialization strategy - DO NOT extend without field validation
For PFT#9: Case #2675 uses 120.9 days vs Case #845 uses 65.5 days - longer dormancy in optimized case but still fails ecosystem function
Completely opposite nutrient strategies work for PFT#7. Case #2678 uses 84,000x higher Vmax (2.14e-5 vs 2.50e-10) with low affinity. Case #845 uses negligible Vmax with high affinity. Both succeed.
Critical for PFT#10 winter survival. Case #845 value of -42.9 C vs Case #2678 value of -97.2 C represents 54.4 C warmer threshold (more tolerant). Less negative = better survival.
Extremely low value (1e-06) means btran must drop to essentially zero to trigger hydraulic mortality, may be too sensitive for Arctic conditions
For PFT#9: increasing from 5.19e-7 to 1.00e-6 provides additional 50-100% improvement by preventing summer drought mortality
Key parameter for fixing PFT#9 mortality trap, modified to 0.30 in all 845 experiments

Paradoxical behavior - lower L:FR (2.37, more fineroot allocation) underestimates fineroot while higher L:FR (9.88, less allocation) matches perfectly. Total productivity matters more than allocation fraction.
For PFT#9: increasing from 0.0153 to 0.045 improves biomass but causes LAI/GPP overshoot - should be avoided or used at lower values
Height allometry shows strong allocation trade-offs for PFT#7 fineroot
Integral gain eliminates persistent C:nutrient errors. Currently fixed at 0 (OFF). Chronic P limitation may benefit from ki > 0 for allocation memory.
Derivative gain provides damping against allocation oscillations. Currently fixed at 0.1, but optimal value may depend on kp magnitude.
Controls root distribution depth affecting nutrient access
For PFT#10: field-calibrated value (11.510) from 25 graminoid cores
Works with prof_a to control root distribution shape and fine-tune vertical nutrient access
For PFT#10: field-calibrated value (6.520) from graminoid root profiles, original Morris bounds too narrow
Controls phosphorus storage ratios for Arctic PFTs
Controls nitrogen storage ratios for Arctic PFTs
Affects C balance for allocation and steady-state leaf biomass. Deciduous PFTs may need shorter longevity.
2-parameter exponential (a,b) achieved best RMSE for evergreen shrubs and graminoids, but calibrated graminoid values still make them more surface-concentrated than biologically correct
For evergreen: calibrated to a=22.341, b=10.355 (3.2x and 6.9x increase from defaults), indicating more surface-concentrated than defaults, consistent with ericoid mycorrhizae strategy
For deciduous: calibrated to a=18.321, b=18.289 (nearly symmetric, 2.6x and 12.2x increase from defaults), showing intermediate surface concentration
Increasing desorption rate can destabilize ecosystem by accelerating P cycling beyond sustainable levels, leading to vulnerability during stress events
Controls rate at which plant-available P becomes mineral-adsorbed. For Gelisols: 0.005 (0.5% per 30 days). High ratio with r_desorp creates strong P retention
Namelist variable pointing to soil chemistry parameter file. Can be overridden in user_nl_elm to test modified soil chemistry parameters
Controls litter decomposition rate based on soil moisture - low values during drought prevent litter breakdown and trap nutrients
Controls maximum hydraulic failure mortality rate - was the dominant mortality factor during 1963-1968 drought for PFT#7
PID integral gain parameter controlling chronic P limitation memory
PID derivative gain parameter for nutrient control
Empirical fractions from Kougarok data: 0-10cm: 34%, 10-20cm: 43% (peak), 20-30cm: 16%, 30-40cm: 7%, preserving subsurface peak biology
Jackson Beta formula performed identically to 2-parameter exponential for deciduous shrubs and achieved 79.8% improvement for graminoids with calibrated a = 0.9171
